IB Chemistry HL
Thermometric Titration of NaOH

How do I use this resource?

a

easy

Explain why a polystyrene cup is used rather than a glass beaker. [1]

Attempt your answer here and get AI feedback


Mark Scheme

polystyrene is a thermal insulator / reduces heat loss to the surroundings ✓\checkmark✓

Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
A calorimeter must keep the released heat in the solution, where the thermometer records it. Polystyrene conducts little heat outward and absorbs almost none itself, so the assumption that only the solution warms is nearly true. A glass beaker conducts heat to the surroundings and absorbs some heat itself; both losses make the reaction appear less exothermic.

b

medium

On Graph 1, draw a line of best fit through the rising temperatures and another through the falling temperatures, and extend them until they meet. Use your lines to determine the equivalence volume and the temperature change, ΔT,\Delta T,ΔT, at the equivalence point. [2]

Attempt your answer here and get AI feedback


Mark Scheme

Veq=11.5 cm3V_{\textrm{eq}} = 11.5 \textrm{\ cm}^3Veq​=11.5 cm3 ✓\checkmark✓
ΔT=8.4 K ✓\Delta T = 8.4 \textrm{\ K} \: \checkmarkΔT=8.4 K✓

Accept VeqV_{\textrm{eq}}Veq​ from 11.2 to 11.8 cm3^\mathit{3}3 and ΔT\Delta TΔT from 8.2 to 8.6 K. \

Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
Neither set of points peaks at the true equivalence point, because heat is lost throughout the titration and the temperature is recorded only after each 1.00 cm31.00 \textrm{\ cm}^31.00 cm3 addition. Each set of points lies close to a straight line, so the two lines are drawn separately and extended until they meet. The intersection gives the equivalence volume, 11.5 cm3,11.5 \textrm{\ cm}^3,11.5 cm3, and the temperature the mixture would have reached with no heat loss, 28.4 ∘C.28.4\,{}^\circ\textrm{C}.28.4∘C. The starting temperature was 20.0 ∘C,20.0\,{}^\circ\textrm{C},20.0∘C, so

ΔT=28.4 ∘C−20.0 ∘C=8.4 K\Delta T = 28.4\,{}^\circ\textrm{C} - 20.0\,{}^\circ\textrm{C} = \answer{8.4 \textrm{\ K}}ΔT=28.4∘C−20.0∘C=8.4 K​

A change of 1 ∘C1\,{}^\circ\textrm{C}1∘C is the same as a change of 1 K,1 \textrm{\ K},1 K, so ΔT\Delta TΔT can be given in either unit.

c

medium

Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide solution. [1]

Attempt your answer here and get AI feedback


Mark Scheme

c(NaOH)=0.920 mol dm−3c(\ce{NaOH}) = 0.920 \textrm{\ mol dm}^{-3}c(NaOH)=0.920 mol dm−3 ✓\checkmark✓

Accept values consistent with VeqV_{\textrm{eq}}Veq​ from part (b), 0.896 to 0.944 mol dm −3^\mathit{\,-3}−3.

Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
At the equivalence point the amount of acid added equals the amount of base present, because NaOH\ce{NaOH}NaOH and HCl\ce{HCl}HCl react in a 1:11 : 11:1 ratio:

n(HCl)=2.00 mol dm−3×0.01150 dm3=0.0230 moln(\ce{HCl}) = 2.00 \textrm{\ mol dm}^{-3} \times 0.01150 \textrm{\ dm}^3 = 0.0230 \textrm{\ mol}n(HCl)=2.00 mol dm−3×0.01150 dm3=0.0230 mol

c(NaOH)=0.0230 mol0.02500 dm3=0.920 mol dm−3c(\ce{NaOH}) = \dfrac{0.0230 \textrm{\ mol}}{0.02500 \textrm{\ dm}^3} = \answer{0.920 \textrm{\ mol dm}^{-3}}c(NaOH)=0.02500 dm30.0230 mol​=0.920 mol dm−3​

d

medium

Outline why the temperature decreases when acid is added beyond the equivalence point. [2]

Attempt your answer here and get AI feedback


Mark Scheme

no further reaction occurs, so no more heat is released ✓\checkmark✓
same heat is shared by a larger mass of solution, so the temperature falls ✓\checkmark✓

Accept the added acid is cooler than the mixture for M2.

Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
Heat is released only while acid reacts with base. Once the base is used up at the equivalence point, the added acid has nothing to react with, so no more heat is produced. Each further addition increases the mass of solution in the cup, and the same amount of heat is now spread over more solution, so the temperature falls. The added acid is also at room temperature, cooler than the warm mixture, so each addition cools the mixture further.

e

hard

Determine the enthalpy of neutralization, in kJ mol−1.\textrm{kJ mol}^{-1}.kJ mol−1. Assume the mixture has the density and specific heat capacity of water; use sections 1 and 2 of the IB Chemistry data booklet.

If you did not obtain values in part (b), use 11.00 cm311.00 \textrm{\ cm}^311.00 cm3 and 8.0 K,8.0 \textrm{\ K},8.0 K, although these are not the correct answers. [2]

Attempt your answer here and get AI feedback


Mark Scheme

q=1.28 kJq = 1.28 \textrm{\ kJ}q=1.28 kJ ✓\checkmark✓
ΔH=−55.7 kJ mol−1\Delta H = -55.7 \textrm{\ kJ mol}^{-1}ΔH=−55.7 kJ mol−1 ✓\checkmark✓

Award [2] for correct final answer.
Accept −-−54.7 kJ mol −1^\mathit{\,-1}−1 from the values 11.00 cm3^\mathit{3}3 and 8.0 K.

Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
The heat released warms the whole mixture at the equivalence point. Assuming a density of 1.00 g cm−3,1.00 \textrm{\ g cm}^{-3},1.00 g cm−3, its mass is

m=(25.00 cm3+11.50 cm3)×1.00 g cm−3=36.5 gm = \left(25.00 \textrm{\ cm}^3 + 11.50 \textrm{\ cm}^3\right) \times 1.00 \textrm{\ g cm}^{-3} = 36.5 \textrm{\ g}m=(25.00 cm3+11.50 cm3)×1.00 g cm−3=36.5 g

The heat absorbed by the mixture, using ΔT\Delta TΔT from part (b), is

q=mcΔT=36.5 g×4.18 J g−1 K−1×8.4 K=1.28×103 J=1.28 kJq = mc\Delta T = 36.5 \textrm{\ g} \times 4.18 \textrm{\ J g}^{-1}\textrm{ K}^{-1} \times 8.4 \textrm{\ K} = 1.28 \times 10^3 \textrm{\ J} = 1.28 \textrm{\ kJ}q=mcΔT=36.5 g×4.18 J g−1 K−1×8.4 K=1.28×103 J=1.28 kJ

The amount of water formed equals the amount of acid added at the equivalence point:

n(HX2O)=n(HCl)=2.00 mol dm−3×0.01150 dm3=0.0230 moln(\ce{H2O}) = n(\ce{HCl}) = 2.00 \textrm{\ mol dm}^{-3} \times 0.01150 \textrm{\ dm}^3 = 0.0230 \textrm{\ mol}n(HX2​O)=n(HCl)=2.00 mol dm−3×0.01150 dm3=0.0230 mol

The reaction released the heat that the mixture absorbed, so ΔH\Delta HΔH is negative:

ΔH=−qn=−1.28 kJ0.0230 mol=−55.7 kJ mol−1\Delta H = -\dfrac{q}{n} = -\dfrac{1.28 \textrm{\ kJ}}{0.0230 \textrm{\ mol}} = \answer{-55.7 \textrm{\ kJ mol}^{-1}}ΔH=−nq​=−0.0230 mol1.28 kJ​=−55.7 kJ mol−1​

 \  

f

hard

Suggest why the extrapolated temperature change gives a more valid value of the enthalpy of neutralization than the highest recorded temperature. [1]

Attempt your answer here and get AI feedback


Mark Scheme

extrapolation estimates the temperature the mixture would have reached with no heat loss «during the addition», whereas the highest recorded temperature is reached after some heat has already been lost ✓\checkmark✓

Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
By the time the highest temperature is recorded, the cup has been losing heat for several minutes, so the recorded change, 28.0 ∘C−20.0 ∘C=8.0 K,28.0\,{}^\circ\textrm{C} - 20.0\,{}^\circ\textrm{C} = 8.0 \textrm{\ K},28.0∘C−20.0∘C=8.0 K, is smaller than the change that would occur with no heat loss. The intersection of the two lines estimates the temperature at the moment the reaction is complete, as if all the heat had been released before any was lost.

Introduction

A student determined the concentration of a sodium hydroxide solution by thermometric titration. A 25.00 cm325.00 \textrm{\ cm}^325.00 cm3 portion of NaOH(aq)\ce{NaOH}\textrm{(aq)}NaOH(aq) was placed in a polystyrene cup and 2.00 mol dm−32.00 \textrm{\ mol dm}^{-3}2.00 mol dm−3 hydrochloric acid was added 1.00 cm31.00 \textrm{\ cm}^31.00 cm3 at a time from a burette, stirring and recording the steady temperature after each addition.

Introduction
​

Introduction

A student determined the concentration of a sodium hydroxide solution by thermometric titration. A 25.00 cm325.00 \textrm{\ cm}^325.00 cm3 portion of NaOH(aq)\ce{NaOH}\textrm{(aq)}NaOH(aq) was placed in a polystyrene cup and 2.00 mol dm−32.00 \textrm{\ mol dm}^{-3}2.00 mol dm−3 hydrochloric acid was added 1.00 cm31.00 \textrm{\ cm}^31.00 cm3 at a time from a burette, stirring and recording the steady temperature after each addition.

Graph 1: Temperature vs. Volume of HCl

Graph 1: Temperature of the mixture vs. volume of HCl(aq)\ce{HCl}\textrm{(aq)}HCl(aq) added.
